settings.heading: Patio vs Deck: The Difference Between a Deck and a Patio & How to Decide
settings.lede: A patio covers the ground. A deck gives you a level, dry outdoor living space that starts at your back door, and its upkeep stays on the surface where you can see it. Here’s how a deck and a patio compare on build, maintenance, durability and resale value.
settings.image_alt: A-DIY composite deck beside a stone patio with lounge seating

settings.eyebrow: It starts at the back door
settings.heading: It starts with one small moment: coffee in hand, back door open, stepping out into your own backyard.
settings.body: For a lot of homes, that moment never feels quite right. The door sits a step too high above the lawn. The yard tilts toward the fence. The grass stays soft for days after rain. So the chairs stay folded, and the backyard waits for a better day.
settings.payoff: A patio has to be dug into that ground to fix it. A deck simply rises above it, meeting your door so your first step lands on a level, dry floor. It’s there for the slow morning coffee, the long summer dinner and the evening you didn’t plan to stay out so late, season after season.
settings.image_alt: A-DIY wood deck with steps that meets the back door

settings.heading: Deck or patio: which is better for your backyard?
settings.lead: For most backyards, a deck is the more reliable long-term choice.
settings.body: Choose a deck if your yard slopes, your door sits above the ground, the soil holds water, or you want upkeep you can plan for. Choose a patio if your yard is flat, firm and drains well, and you want a hard surface at ground level. Like the low look of a patio? A ground-level deck gives you both.

settings.heading: Deck vs. Patio: What Works Best for Your Backyard?
settings.intro: From installation and maintenance to durability and cost, see how decks and patios compare and why a deck may be the better fit for your backyard.
settings.deck_image_alt: A-DIY composite deck with a pergola
settings.deck_desc: Wood or composite boards on a frame and footings
settings.patio_desc: Pavers, concrete or stone laid on the ground
settings.takeaway: If your yard is flat and dry, a patio does the job. If it slopes, sits low, stays wet, or you want a true outdoor room, a deck is the better backyard.

settings.label: Best yard
settings.deck: Slopes, dips, raised doorways and soggy ground

settings.label: Height
settings.deck: Built to meet your door threshold
settings.patio: Sits at ground level, often a step down

settings.label: After it rains
settings.deck: Water drains between the boards and furniture stays off wet soil
settings.patio: Needs the right slope and base so water doesn’t pool

settings.label: What the build involves
settings.deck: Footings, a frame and boards, so the yard stays as it is
settings.patio: Excavation and a compacted gravel base, then pavers or concrete

settings.label: Upkeep
settings.deck: Wood: clean and reseal every 2–3 years. Composite: wash once or twice a year
settings.patio: Pavers: weed and re-sand joints; sunken spots mean lifting stones to rebuild the base. Concrete: reseal and patch cracks

settings.label: Lifespan
settings.deck: Wood: 20+ years with resealing. Composite: 25–30 years
settings.patio: Pavers: 30–50 years. Concrete: 25–50 years, if the base holds

settings.label: Adding on later
settings.deck: Add steps or railings when you’re ready
settings.patio: Concrete is permanent; pavers have to be lifted and relaid

settings.label: Resale data
settings.deck: Wood deck recouped 94.9% of its cost; composite 88.5% (2025 Cost vs Value)
settings.patio: 50% return, drops as the patio gets older.

settings.heading: 10 Years Later: Deck vs. Patio
settings.intro: Both can still be standing at year 10. What separates a paver or concrete patio from a backyard deck is how each one ages, and where the work happens when something needs fixing.
settings.cta_title:
A patio’s repairs happen underground.
A deck’s upkeep stays on the surface.
settings.cta_text: Build the deck you’ll still love in ten years. A-DIY composite kits come with a 25-year board warranty.
settings.sources: Sources: NAHB Study of Life Expectancy of Home Components; InterNACHI Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart; JLC 2025 Cost vs. Value report (national averages). Lifespans vary with climate, installation and upkeep.

settings.heading: Love the low look of a patio? Meet the ground-level deck.
settings.body: A ground-level, or floating, deck sits just above the grass on footings instead of being dug into it. You keep the relaxed, close-to-the-yard feel people love about patios, and gain a flat, drained, finished floor. It’s also the easiest kind of deck to build yourself.
settings.note_text: A low deck can often sit over a sound, well-drained slab. Check it isn’t cracked or heaving, and that your local code allows it.
settings.image_alt: Ground-level floating composite deck kit sitting just above the lawn

settings.heading: Why a patio starts with digging, and a deck doesn’t
settings.intro: Both give you outdoor space, but they’re built very differently. A patio is set into the ground, which means digging, gravel, and prep work. An A-DIY deck is built on footings above the soil, so your yard stays intact and the process is simpler.
settings.image_alt: Diagram comparing a patio and an A-DIY deck. A patio is set into the ground: dig it out, build a gravel and sand base, then lay pavers or concrete. An A-DIY deck is built on top of it: deck surface, engineered frame, joists and beams on Tuff Block footings above ground. No digging, a faster build (typically 8–16 hours with 2 adults) and less mess. In one line: a patio changes your ground; a deck sits on top of it.

settings.heading: A deck, without waiting on a contractor
settings.intro: A-DIY ready-to-assemble (prefab) deck kits are professionally engineered so homeowners can build a solid, beautiful deck themselves. Every kit arrives with the framing, boards, hardware, footings and a custom drill bit, so the only tool you bring is a drill.

settings.heading: The Deck Gets The Compliments. The Experience Earns The Reviews.
Deck vs patio, Faqs
settings.intro: Still weighing it up? A deck specialist can look at your yard with you.

settings.question: What is the difference between a deck and a patio?
settings.answer: A deck is a raised platform of wood or composite boards on a frame, supported by footings. A patio is a paved surface, such as concrete, pavers or stone, laid directly on prepared ground.

settings.question: Is a deck considered a patio?
settings.answer: No. A deck is a raised platform of wood or composite boards on a frame and footings. A patio is a hard surface, such as pavers, concrete or stone, laid on the ground. A ground-level deck can sit as low as a patio, but it’s still a deck.

settings.question: Which lasts longer, a deck or a patio?
settings.answer: A paver patio can last 30–50 years and concrete 25–50, as long as the base holds. A wood deck typically lasts 10–20+ years with regular resealing, and composite decking 25–30 years. The bigger difference is upkeep: a patio’s problems start underground, while a deck’s wear stays on the surface where it’s easy to fix.

settings.question: Is a deck or a patio easier to maintain?
settings.answer: A composite deck is the easiest: wash it once or twice a year. A wood deck needs cleaning and resealing every 2–3 years. A paver patio needs weeding and re-sanding, and sunken areas mean lifting stones and rebuilding the base.

settings.question: Deck or patio: which adds more resale value to a home?
settings.answer: Yes, a deck adds value to a home, and decks have the clearer data. In the 2025 Cost vs Value report, a wood deck addition recouped 94.9% of its cost at resale nationally, and a composite deck recouped 88.5%. Patios aren’t included in that report, so there’s no comparable national figure.

settings.question: Deck vs patio vs porch vs balcony: what’s the difference?
settings.answer: A deck is an open platform on footings, usually off the back of the house. A porch is a covered space attached to the house, typically at an entrance. A balcony is an elevated platform on an upper floor that you reach from inside. In most backyards, the real choice is between a deck and a patio.

settings.question: Deck vs pavers: which works better on a sloped yard?
settings.answer: A deck. Its footings set the height, so the floor stays level while the ground slopes underneath. Pavers need a flat, compacted base, so a paver patio on a slope usually means regrading or retaining walls.

settings.question: Concrete patio vs wood or composite deck: which is better?
settings.answer: It depends on your ground. A concrete patio needs a flat, well-prepared base and is permanent once poured. A wood deck stands on footings, handles slopes and damp soil, and feels softer underfoot. Wood needs cleaning and resealing now and then; composite just needs cleaning.

settings.question: Raised patio vs deck: which is easier to build?
settings.answer: Usually the deck. A raised patio needs retaining walls and compacted fill to hold the surface up. A deck holds itself up on footings and a frame, and an A-DIY kit goes together with a drill, with no cutting or measuring.

settings.question: Floating deck vs patio: is a ground-level deck better?
settings.answer: It depends on what you want underfoot. A floating (ground-level) deck and a patio both sit low to the yard, but the deck adds a finished, drained floor that feels softer than stone and needs no excavation. A patio gives you a hard surface for a grill or fire pit.

settings.question: Can you build a deck over a concrete patio?
settings.answer: Often, yes. A low deck can sit over a sound, well-drained slab. Check that the concrete isn’t cracked or heaving, that water can still run off, and that your local code allows it.

settings.question: Can I build a deck myself without special tools?
settings.answer: Yes. A-DIY kits are engineered so there’s no cutting or measuring. A power drill is the only tool you need, and the custom drill bit comes in the box.

settings.question: Do I need a permit to build a deck?
settings.answer: It depends on your town. Some codes exempt low, freestanding decks under a set height and size; others don’t. Check with your local building department before you build.

settings.question: What comes in an A-DIY deck kit?
settings.answer: Engineered framing (beams and joists), deck boards, galvanized screws and hardware, Tuff Block footings, a custom drill bit and a step-by-step assembly guide.
